takeaways: Concrete is graded by its characteristic cube strength; its design curve is a parabola to a strain of 0.002 and flat at 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> to 0.0035.
HYSD steel reaches its design stress 0.87f<sub>y</sub> only at a strain of 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/Es + 0.002 (0.0038 for Fe415); this strain sets the limiting neutral axis depth.
Creep (θ = 2.2, 1.6, 1.1 at 7 days, 28 days, one year) and shrinkage (0.0003) add long-term deflection, not strength.
The working stress method keeps elastic service stresses under permissible values, with m = 280/(3σ<sub>cbc</sub>) and the constants k, j and Q.
The ultimate load method puts all the safety on the load through one factor and designs for collapse, but checks nothing at service.
Limit state design checks collapse with factored loads and design strengths, and serviceability with service loads, using characteristic values and partial safety factors.
Characteristic strength is μ − 1.65σ and characteristic load is μ + 1.65σ; the partial factors γ<sub>f</sub> (1.5, 1.2, 0.9) and γ<sub>m</sub> (1.5, 1.15) turn them into design values.
The stress block gives C = 0.36f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> at 0.42x<sub>u</sub>; with x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.48 for Fe415 the limiting moment is 0.138f<sub>ck</sub> b d².
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the comparison of the three design methods with the advantages of the limit state method, the WSM design of a singly reinforced beam, and the IS 456 values of characteristic strength, partial safety factors and the stress block. Analysis and design of singly and doubly reinforced beams by the limit state method is taught in full with limit state design of beams; the singly reinforced questions here use only this unit's stress block.

bank.q: Explain the stress–strain behaviour of concrete and of reinforcing steel (mild steel and HYSD bars). Sketch the design curves of IS 456 and state the numbers that define them.
outline: Concrete: cube strength, grades, real curve with peak near 0.002 and falling branch
IS 456 design curve: parabola to 0.002, flat at 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> to 0.0035
E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub>
Mild steel: sharp yield, bilinear design curve at 0.87f<sub>y</sub>
HYSD bars: 0.2 % proof stress, curve leaves the straight line at 0.8 × 0.87f<sub>y</sub>, reaches 0.87f<sub>y</sub> at 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/Es + 0.002
E<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm²; creep and shrinkage values
answer: Concrete is graded by its characteristic cube strength f<sub>ck</sub>, the 28-day strength of 150 mm cubes below which not more than 5 % of results fall: M20 has f<sub>ck</sub> = 20 N/mm². Its tensile strength is about a tenth of this and is ignored in design.

Real curve of concrete in compression: stress rises almost linearly at first, bends over as micro-cracks grow, peaks at a strain of about 0.002 and then falls; crushing in a beam occurs near a strain of 0.0035. There is no clear elastic limit, so the modulus is quoted as a short-term value E<sub>c</sub> = 5000√f<sub>ck</sub> (25,000 N/mm² for M25), and the flexural tensile strength as f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7√f<sub>ck</sub> (3.5 N/mm² for M25).

answer.text: IS 456 design curve for concrete: a parabola from zero to a strain of 0.002, then a horizontal line to the ultimate strain 0.0035. The flat part is at 0.67f<sub>ck</sub> in the member and at 0.67f<sub>ck</sub>/γm = 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> for design. For M25:

answer: Mild steel (Fe250) has a sharp yield point and a long yield plateau before strain hardening. Its IS 456 design curve is elastic–perfectly plastic: a straight line with slope E<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm² up to 0.87f<sub>y</sub> = 217.5 N/mm² (strain 0.00109), then flat.

answer.text: HYSD bars (Fe415, Fe500) have no sharp yield point; f<sub>y</sub> is the 0.2 % proof stress. The design curve is straight up to 0.8 × 0.87f<sub>y</sub> and then curves, reaching 0.87f<sub>y</sub> at an extra inelastic strain of 0.002. The SP 16 values for Fe415 are:

answer: So Fe415 reaches its design stress 361 N/mm² only at a strain of 0.0038, and Fe500 at 0.87 × 500/200,000 + 0.002 = 0.00418. These strains fix the limiting neutral axis depth (0.48d and 0.46d).

Ductility: higher grades are stronger but less ductile (minimum elongation 14.5 % for Fe415, 12 % for Fe500). The plateau or long inelastic range of steel is what gives a reinforced concrete beam its visible warning before failure.
Time effects in concrete: creep coefficient 2.2, 1.6 and 1.1 for loading at 7 days, 28 days and one year; shrinkage strain 0.0003. They are used for long-term deflection, not for strength.

Sketch: draw the concrete curve (parabola, flat top, 0.002 and 0.0035 marked, 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> labelled) and the two steel curves on one strain axis (Fe250 bilinear at 217.5 N/mm²; Fe415 straight to 289 N/mm², curved to 361 N/mm² at 0.0038), as in the figure of the chapter on properties of concrete and steel.

Check: at the strain of 0.0035, where concrete crushes, Fe415 bars at the limiting depth are at 0.0038: both materials reach their design limits together, which is the definition of the balanced section in limit state design.

bank.q: Compare the working stress method, the ultimate load method and the limit state method. State the advantages of the limit state method over the other two.
outline: WSM: service loads, elastic behaviour, permissible stresses, modular ratio
ULM: load factor, inelastic strength at failure, no serviceability check
LSM: limit states of collapse and serviceability, characteristic values, partial safety factors
Comparison table
Numerical illustration of economy
Advantages of LSM
answer: Working stress method (WSM): the member is analysed under service loads with no load factor. Concrete and steel are assumed elastic, concrete carries no tension, and steel is converted to concrete with the modular ratio m = 280/(3σ<sub>cbc</sub>). Computed stresses must not exceed permissible stresses, for example σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 7 N/mm² for M20 and σ<sub>st</sub> = 230 N/mm² for Fe415. Safety is the ratio of strength to permissible stress.

Ultimate load method (ULM): service loads are multiplied by a load factor (for example 1.5) and the section is designed to fail only at that load, using the real inelastic strength of concrete and steel with no material factor. Safety is the load factor.

Limit state method (LSM): a limit state is a condition beyond which the member no longer serves its purpose. The member is checked for the limit states of collapse (flexure, compression, shear, torsion) with factored loads and design strengths, and for the limit states of serviceability (deflection, cracking) with service loads. Loads and strengths start from characteristic values (5 % fractiles) and are modified by partial safety factors: γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.5 for dead plus live load, γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel.

Numerical illustration: a balanced section 230 mm wide with d = 450 mm in M20 and Fe415. WSM: M<sub>R</sub> = 0.913 × 230 × 450² = 42.5 kNm at service. LSM: M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 230 × 450² = 128.5 kNm at factored load, that is 128.5/1.5 = 85.7 kNm at service. The same concrete section carries about 2.0 times the service moment by LSM, with more steel.
Advantage 1: LSM checks both safety and serviceability; WSM never computes the collapse load and ULM never checks deflection or cracking.

Advantage 2: separate factors for each load and each material place safety where the uncertainty is: a larger factor on concrete (site-made) than on steel (factory-made), and a dead load factor of 0.9 where dead load helps stability.
Advantage 3: it uses the inelastic reserve of the materials, so sections are smaller and cheaper, as the 2.0 ratio above shows.
Advantage 4: its characteristic values rest on the measured scatter of strengths and loads, so the margin of safety is rational and can be calibrated.
Limitations: more calculation and more checks; reliance on the code's factors; and the serviceability checks become essential because LSM sections are slimmer.
Conclusion: IS 456:2000 uses LSM as its main method and keeps WSM in Annex B for special cases such as liquid-retaining structures and quick checks.

bank.q: Define characteristic strength and characteristic load. Explain their statistical basis, and explain how partial safety factors convert them into design values, with the IS 456 values.
outline: Scatter of test results, normal distribution, mean and standard deviation
f<sub>ck</sub> = μ − 1.65σ; target mean strength f<sub>ck</sub> + 1.65s; IS 456 assumed s
Characteristic load: 95 % probability of not being exceeded; Q<sub>k</sub> = μ + 1.65σ; IS 875 loads
Design load γ<sub>f</sub> F<sub>k</sub> and design strength f<sub>k</sub>/γm
IS 456 Table 18 values; γ<sub>m</sub> 1.5 and 1.15
Design strengths 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> and 0.87f<sub>y</sub>
answer: Strengths and loads scatter. Thirty cubes from one mix give thirty different strengths, roughly in a normal (bell) distribution with a mean μ and a standard deviation σ. Design must not use the mean, because half the concrete would be weaker than assumed.

Characteristic strength (IS 456): the strength below which not more than 5 % of test results are expected to fall. For a normal distribution the 5 % point is 1.645σ below the mean, rounded to 1.65: f<sub>ck</sub> = μ − 1.65σ. Example: μ = 32 N/mm², σ = 4 N/mm² gives f<sub>ck</sub> = 32 − 6.6 = 25.4 N/mm², so M25.

Used backwards for mix design, the target mean strength is f<sub>ck</sub> + 1.65s. IS 456 Table 8 gives assumed s of 3.5 N/mm² (M10, M15), 4.0 N/mm² (M20, M25) and 5.0 N/mm² (M30 to M50). For M25: 25 + 1.65 × 4 = 31.6 N/mm².

Characteristic load (IS 456): the load with a 95 % probability of not being exceeded during the life of the structure: Q<sub>k</sub> = μ<sub>Q</sub> + 1.65σ<sub>Q</sub> (the upper tail, because a high load is unsafe). Example: μ<sub>Q</sub> = 2.4 kN/m², σ<sub>Q</sub> = 0.6 kN/m² gives Q<sub>k</sub> = 3.39 kN/m². Since data are seldom available, the loads of IS 875 and IS 1893 are taken as characteristic loads.

Partial safety factors turn characteristic values into design values: design load F<sub>d</sub> = γ<sub>f</sub> F<sub>k</sub> and design strength f<sub>d</sub> = f<sub>k</sub>/γm. γ<sub>f</sub> allows for loads above the characteristic value, errors in analysis and the consequence of failure; γ<sub>m</sub> for lower strength in the structure than in test specimens and for workmanship.
The 0.9 on dead load is for cases where dead load helps resist wind uplift or overturning. Wind is taken in both directions.

Material factors: γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel at collapse, 1.0 for both at serviceability; for accidental loads 1.2 and 1.0. Steel is factory-made and tested, so it has the smaller factor.

Design strengths: concrete in the member is taken as 0.67f<sub>ck</sub>, so its design value is 0.67f<sub>ck</sub>/1.5 = 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> (11.15 N/mm² for M25); steel 0.87f<sub>y</sub> (361 N/mm² for Fe415).
Check with numbers: a beam with characteristic loads 20 kN/m dead and 12 kN/m imposed has a design load of 1.5 × 32 = 48 kN/m for collapse and 32 kN/m for serviceability.

bank.q: Explain the limit state philosophy as given in IS 456. Describe the limit states of collapse and of serviceability, with the code's limits on deflection and crack width.
outline: Definition of limit state and aim of design
Characteristic values and partial safety factors; S<sub>d</sub> ≤ R<sub>d</sub>
Collapse: flexure, compression, shear, torsion; factored loads and design strengths
Serviceability: deflection span/250 and span/350 or 20 mm; cracks 0.3 mm, 0.2 mm, 0.004 × cover
Loads and factors used for each
Example check
answer: A limit state is a condition beyond which a structure or a member no longer satisfies a design requirement. The aim of design is a structure that, with an acceptable probability, remains fit for use during its life, carries all loads likely to occur, and resists misuse and fire adequately.

The probability is controlled through characteristic values (5 % fractiles of strength, 95 % non-exceedance of load) and partial safety factors. For every limit state the check is design action S<sub>d</sub> ≤ design resistance R<sub>d</sub>.

Limit states of collapse: flexure (bending failure, with tension steel yielding before the concrete crushes for warning), compression (column crushing, with bending and slenderness), shear (diagonal tension, brittle, needing stirrups) and torsion (twisting with shear and bending). Loss of equilibrium of the structure as a whole and failure in fire are also limit states of safety.

For collapse, loads are factored (γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.5 on DL + IL; 1.2 on each of DL, IL and WL; 1.5 or 0.9 on DL with 1.5 WL) and strengths are design values with γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.5 for concrete and 1.15 for steel.
Limit states of serviceability are checked with γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.0 (0.8 on IL and WL when they act together with DL) and γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.0.

Deflection: the final deflection due to all loads, including creep and shrinkage, measured from the supports, must not exceed span/250; the deflection after partitions and finishes are built must not exceed span/350 or 20 mm, whichever is less. In design this is normally ensured by span/effective depth ratios: 7 for cantilevers, 20 for simply supported and 26 for continuous members, with modification factors.

Cracking: surface crack width generally not more than 0.3 mm; 0.2 mm where cracking is harmful because the member is always wet or in contact with soil or ground water; and 0.004 times the nominal cover in particularly aggressive (severe) environments.
Other serviceability limits: vibration, durability (minimum grade, cover, water–cement ratio for the exposure) and fire resistance (minimum dimensions and cover).

answer.text: Example: a 6 m beam with a calculated final deflection of 22 mm and 19 mm after partitions:

answer: The beam is strong enough but fails a serviceability limit, which is exactly why IS 456 checks both families: collapse protects life, serviceability protects use and durability.

bank.q: Design a simply supported rectangular beam of effective span 6 m by the working stress method. It carries a superimposed service load of 20 kN/m besides its self-weight. Width 300 mm, effective cover 50 mm, M25 concrete and Fe415 steel. Check the stresses.
outline: Permissible stresses and m
Design constants k, j, Q
Assume depth, self-weight, service moment
Required d and check
A<sub>st</sub>, minimum steel, choice of bars
Actual neutral axis and stress check
Sketch of section
answer: Permissible stresses (IS 456 Annex B): σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 8.5 N/mm² for M25, σ<sub>st</sub> = 230 N/mm² for Fe415. Modular ratio m = 280/(3 × 8.5) = 10.98.

Method: WSM uses service loads with no load factor, elastic stresses, no tension in concrete and the modular ratio for the steel; the section is sized so that both stresses stay within the permissible values and close to the balanced state.

First trial D = 600 mm (span/10): self-weight 0.3 × 0.6 × 25 = 4.5 kN/m, w = 24.5 kN/m, M = 24.5 × 6²/8 = 110.3 kNm, required d = √(110.3 × 10⁶/(1.109 × 300)) = 576 mm. Provided d = 600 − 50 = 550 mm is not enough.
Provide 3 bars of 20 mm: A<sub>st</sub> = 3 × 314.2 = 942.5 mm² (≥ 897 and < 960, so the section stays under-reinforced).

answer.text: Stress check. Neutral axis from 300x²/2 = 10.98 × 942.5 × (600 − x), i.e. 150x² + 10,349x − 6,209,300 = 0:

answer: Sketch: a 300 mm × 650 mm rectangle with 3 bars of 20 mm at 600 mm from the top, two hanger bars of 12 mm at the top to hold the stirrups, and 8 mm stirrups (shear design is done separately).

Detailing: clear cover 25 mm to the stirrups with 8 mm stirrups gives 25 + 8 + 10 = 43 mm to the bar centre; the 50 mm effective cover adopted is on the safe side. Clear spacing of three 20 mm bars in 300 mm: (300 − 2 × 33 − 3 × 20)/2 = 87 mm, more than the bar size and the aggregate size plus 5 mm, so the bars fit in one layer.
Check: span/d = 6000/600 = 10, well below the basic 20, so deflection is unlikely to govern; both stresses are within the permissible values, so the design is adequate in flexure by WSM.

bank.q: A rectangular beam 250 mm wide with an effective depth of 450 mm has 3 bars of 16 mm of Fe415 as tension steel in M25 concrete. By the working stress method find (a) the neutral axis depth and the type of section, (b) the moment of resistance, and (c) the stresses under a service moment of 50 kNm.
outline: Permissible stresses and m
Actual neutral axis from first moments of area
Critical neutral axis and type of section
Moment of resistance from the governing material
Stresses under the given moment
Comment
answer: Data: b = 250 mm, d = 450 mm, A<sub>st</sub> = 3 × 201.1 = 603 mm²; σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 8.5 N/mm², σ<sub>st</sub> = 230 N/mm², m = 280/(3 × 8.5) = 10.98.

Method: in elastic analysis the neutral axis depends only on the section and m, not on the load. Find x from the first moments of the transformed section, compare it with the critical depth x<sub>c</sub> = k d to see which material reaches its permissible stress first, then take moments about the force of the other material.

answer.text: Neutral axis: b x²/2 = m A<sub>st</sub> (d − x):

answer: Critical neutral axis x<sub>c</sub> = k d = 0.2887 × 450 = 129.9 mm. Since x = 130.2 mm is just above x<sub>c</sub>, the section is (very slightly) over-reinforced, so concrete governs. The two are within 0.3 mm, so the section is practically balanced.

Moment of resistance (concrete governs): M<sub>R</sub> = ½ σ<sub>cbc</sub> b x z = 0.5 × 8.5 × 250 × 130.2 × 406.6 = 56.2 × 10⁶ N mm = 56.2 kNm. (For comparison, with steel at 230 N/mm²: 230 × 603 × 406.6 = 56.4 kNm; the smaller value governs.)

answer.text: Stresses under M = 50 kNm (the neutral axis does not move with the moment in elastic analysis):

answer: Check by the strain diagram: σ<sub>st</sub>/m should equal σ<sub>cbc</sub> × (d − x)/x: 203.9/10.98 = 18.57 and 7.56 × 319.8/130.2 = 18.57. Correct.
Forces under 50 kNm: C = ½ × 7.56 × 250 × 130.2 = 123,000 N and T = 603 × 203.9 = 123,000 N; equal, as they must be, and 123,000 × 406.6 = 50.0 × 10⁶ N mm, the applied moment.
If the beam had only 2 bars of 16 mm (402 mm²), x would fall below x<sub>c</sub> and steel would govern: the type of section follows from the steel area, not from the load.

Comment: the beam can carry 56.2 kNm at service; under 50 kNm both stresses are within their limits. Because x and x<sub>c</sub> are almost equal, both materials are used almost fully, which is the aim of WSM design.

bank.q: A singly reinforced beam 300 mm wide with an effective depth of 500 mm has 4 bars of 20 mm of Fe415 in M20 concrete. Find its ultimate moment of resistance by the limit state method, state whether it is under-reinforced, and compare it with the limiting moment and with the strength found without material factors.
outline: Design strengths
Neutral axis from C = T
Compare with x<sub>u,max</sub>
M<sub>u</sub> from force × lever arm, check with IS 456 formula
M<sub>u,lim</sub>
Comparison with ultimate load method value
answer: Data: b = 300 mm, d = 500 mm, A<sub>st</sub> = 4 × 314.2 = 1257 mm², f<sub>ck</sub> = 20 N/mm², f<sub>y</sub> = 415 N/mm².

Method: at the limit state of collapse the concrete carries the stress block force 0.36f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> at 0.42x<sub>u</sub> below the top; if the section is under-reinforced the steel carries 0.87f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub>. Find x<sub>u</sub> from C = T, confirm x<sub>u</sub> ≤ x<sub>u,max</sub>, then M<sub>u</sub> = T × lever arm.
Steel force at the design stress: T = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> = 0.87 × 415 × 1257 = 453,700 N.
Concrete force C = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub>. Setting C = T: x<sub>u</sub> = 453,700/(0.36 × 20 × 300) = 453,700/2160 = 210.1 mm.
x<sub>u,max</sub> = 0.48 d = 240 mm for Fe415. Since 210.1 < 240, the section is under-reinforced: the steel yields first and the failure is ductile.
Strain check: steel strain = 0.0035 × (500 − 210.1)/210.1 = 0.00483, more than the 0.0038 Fe415 needs to reach 0.87f<sub>y</sub>, so the assumed steel stress is correct.

Check with IS 456 G-1.1: M<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> d (1 − A<sub>st</sub> f<sub>y</sub>/(b d f<sub>ck</sub>)) = 0.87 × 415 × 1257 × 500 × (1 − 1257 × 415/(300 × 500 × 20)) = 226.9 × 10⁶ × 0.8261 = 187.4 kNm, within 0.3 % of the first result.
Limiting moment: M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² = 0.138 × 20 × 300 × 500² = 207.0 kNm. The beam uses 186.8/207.0 = 90 % of it.

answer.text: Comparison with the ultimate load method (materials at full strength, as in the chapter on that method):

answer: The ratio 226.0/186.8 = 1.21 is the extra margin that the material factors build into the limit state resistance; the load factor 1.5 then acts on top of it.

Sketch: the section with 4 bars at d = 500 mm, the strain line from 0.0035 at the top to 0.00483 at the steel through the neutral axis at 210 mm, and the stress block with C = 453.7 kN at 0.42 × 210.1 = 88.2 mm and T = 453.7 kN, as in the stress block figure.

Answer: M<sub>u</sub> = 186.8 kNm, under-reinforced (x<sub>u</sub> = 210 mm < 240 mm), below M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 207 kNm. As a design check, the beam can carry a factored moment of 186.8 kNm, that is a service moment of 186.8/1.5 = 124.5 kNm.

bank.q: Derive the stress block parameters of IS 456 for the limit state of collapse in flexure, and derive x<sub>u,max</sub>/d and M<sub>u,lim</sub> for Fe415 and Fe500 steel.
outline: Assumptions of IS 456 for flexure
Strain diagram and position of strain 0.002
Area of the stress block: 0.36f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>
Centroid: 0.42x<sub>u</sub>
Steel strain at 0.87f<sub>y</sub> and x<sub>u,max</sub>/d
M<sub>u,lim</sub> = R b d²
answer: Assumptions: plane sections remain plane; maximum strain in concrete at the outermost compression fibre 0.0035; concrete tensile strength ignored; concrete stress follows the parabola–rectangle design curve with peak 0.67f<sub>ck</sub>/1.5 = 0.446f<sub>ck</sub>; steel follows its design curve with 0.87f<sub>y</sub>; the tension steel strain at failure is at least 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/Es + 0.002.

Strain diagram: zero at the neutral axis (depth x<sub>u</sub>) and 0.0035 at the top. The strain 0.002 is at 0.002/0.0035 = 4/7 of x<sub>u</sub> above the neutral axis, that is at 3/7 x<sub>u</sub> below the top. The stress is constant at 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> from the top to 3/7 x<sub>u</sub>, and parabolic from there to zero at the neutral axis.

answer.pre:
rectangle   = k × (3/7) x<sub>u</sub>          = 0.4286 k x<sub>u</sub>
parabola    = (2/3) × k × (4/7) x<sub>u</sub>  = 0.3810 k x<sub>u</sub>
total       = (17/21) k x<sub>u</sub>         = 0.8095 × 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub> = 0.361f<sub>ck</sub> x<sub>u</sub>
C = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub>

answer.text: Position of C below the top:
answer.pre:
rectangle: centroid at (3/14) x<sub>u</sub> = 0.2143 x<sub>u</sub>
parabola:  centroid at 3/7 x<sub>u</sub> + (3/8)(4/7) x<sub>u</sub> = (9/14) x<sub>u</sub> = 0.6429 x<sub>u</sub>
x̄ = (0.4286 × 0.2143 + 0.3810 × 0.6429) / 0.8095 = 0.416 x<sub>u</sub> ≈ 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>

answer: So the lever arm is z = d − 0.42x<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>u</sub> = 0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> (d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>).

Limiting neutral axis: for steel to reach 0.87f<sub>y</sub> when concrete crushes, its strain must be ε<sub>s</sub> = 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/Es + 0.002. From similar triangles x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.0035/(0.0035 + ε<sub>s</sub>).
Hence M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² for Fe415 and 0.133 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² for Fe500 (and 0.148 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² for Fe250, with x<sub>u,max</sub>/d = 0.53).

Check with a beam: 230 mm × 450 mm effective, M25, Fe415: x<sub>u,max</sub> = 216 mm, C = 0.36 × 25 × 230 × 216 = 447,120 N, z = 359.3 mm, M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 160.6 kNm, and 0.138 × 25 × 230 × 450² = 160.7 kNm: the constant reproduces the force–lever-arm result.

bank.q: A hall beam of span 8 m carries a characteristic dead load of 18 kN/m and an imposed load of 10 kN/m; it is made of concrete whose cube results have a mean of 31 N/mm² and a standard deviation of 3.6 N/mm², with Fe500 bars. Find the characteristic and design strengths of both materials, the design moment and shear for collapse, and the service moment.
outline: f<sub>ck</sub> from mean and standard deviation, grade
Design strengths 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> and 0.87f<sub>y</sub>
Factored load 1.5(DL + IL)
Design moment and shear
Service load and moment
Units and checks
answer: Characteristic concrete strength: f<sub>ck</sub> = μ − 1.65σ = 31 − 1.65 × 3.6 = 31 − 5.94 = 25.06 N/mm². This is at least 25, so the concrete is M25; design uses f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm².
Design compressive strength of concrete in flexure: 0.67 × 25/1.5 = 11.17 N/mm², written 0.446 × 25 = 11.15 N/mm².
Steel: f<sub>y</sub> = 500 N/mm²; design strength 500/1.15 = 434.8 N/mm², written 0.87 × 500 = 435 N/mm².

The loads given are characteristic loads (the IS 875 values are taken as characteristic): each has a 95 % probability of not being exceeded during the life of the hall. Their sum is 18 + 10 = 28 kN/m.
Design load (collapse, DL + IL): w<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × (18 + 10) = 1.5 × 28 = 42 kN/m.
Design moment: M<sub>u</sub> = w<sub>u</sub> L²/8 = 42 × 8²/8 = 336 kNm.
Design shear at the support: Vu = w<sub>u</sub> L/2 = 42 × 8/2 = 168 kN.

Why each factor: γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.5 covers loads above the characteristic value and errors in analysis; γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.5 on concrete and 1.15 on steel cover strength in the structure lower than in the tests. The concrete factor is larger because site concrete scatters more than mill-made steel.
Service load (γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.0): w = 28 kN/m; service moment M = 28 × 64/8 = 224 kNm, which is 336/1.5.

Use of these values: the moment 336 kNm is compared with the design resistance from the stress block (0.36f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> at 0.42x<sub>u</sub>, with 0.87f<sub>y</sub> in the steel), and the service values 224 kNm and 28 kN/m are used for deflection and crack checks with γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.0.

Check: if the site standard deviation had been 4.0 N/mm² (the IS 456 assumed value for M25), f<sub>ck</sub> = 31 − 6.6 = 24.4 N/mm² and the concrete could only be called M20: quality control decides the grade. Units: N/mm² for strengths, kN/m for loads, kNm for moments and kN for shear throughout.

bank.q: Design a simply supported rectangular beam of effective span 5 m by the limit state method. Besides its self-weight it carries a characteristic dead load of 6 kN/m and an imposed load of 10 kN/m. Width 230 mm, M20 concrete, Fe415 steel, effective cover 45 mm.
outline: Loads and factored moment with self-weight
M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b d² gives d
Adopt D and check M<sub>u</sub> ≤ M<sub>u,lim</sub>
A<sub>st</sub> from the IS 456 quadratic
Bars, minimum steel and x<sub>u</sub> check
Moment capacity of the bars provided
answer: Method: find the factored moment including self-weight, size d so that M<sub>u</sub> ≤ M<sub>u,lim</sub> (singly reinforced, ductile), find A<sub>st</sub> from the IS 456 flexure equation, choose bars, and check the moment the bars provide. Design strengths: 0.446f<sub>ck</sub> = 8.92 N/mm² for M20 and 0.87f<sub>y</sub> = 361 N/mm² for Fe415.
Trial overall depth D = 500 mm (span/10). Self-weight = 0.23 × 0.5 × 25 = 2.875 kN/m. Total characteristic load = 6 + 2.875 + 10 = 18.875 kN/m.
Factored load w<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × 18.875 = 28.31 kN/m; factored moment M<sub>u</sub> = 28.31 × 5²/8 = 88.48 kNm.
Required depth for a singly reinforced section: d = √(M<sub>u</sub>/(0.138 f<sub>ck</sub> b)) = √(88.48 × 10⁶/(0.138 × 20 × 230)) = √139,400 = 373 mm.

Provided d = 500 − 45 = 455 mm > 373 mm. M<sub>u,lim</sub> = 0.138 × 20 × 230 × 455² = 131.4 kNm ≥ 88.48 kNm, so the section is singly reinforced and under-reinforced. (The extra depth over 373 mm also helps deflection: span/d = 5000/455 = 11.)

answer.text: Steel area from M<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> A<sub>st</sub> d (1 − A<sub>st</sub> f<sub>y</sub>/(b d f<sub>ck</sub>)), IS 456 G-1.1, solved as:

answer: Minimum steel 0.85 b d/fy = 0.85 × 230 × 455/415 = 214 mm²; 613 mm² governs.
Provide 2 bars of 20 mm: A<sub>st</sub> = 628 mm².

Serviceability: span/d = 5000/455 = 11.0, against a basic value of 20 for a simply supported beam, so deflection is satisfied without a detailed check; bar spacing and cover follow the detailing rules.
Result: beam 230 mm × 500 mm, 2 bars of 20 mm at the bottom (d = 455 mm), with hanger bars and stirrups designed for shear separately. M<sub>u</sub> provided 90.2 kNm against 88.5 kNm required.
Sketch: a 230 mm × 500 mm section, two 20 mm bars at 455 mm from the top, two 10 mm hanger bars at the top and 8 mm two-legged stirrups.
Check: the steel percentage is 100 × 628/(230 × 455) = 0.60 %, well below the limiting 0.96 % for M20 and Fe415, which confirms an under-reinforced, ductile section.

bank.q: The 6 m beam of the working stress design question (300 mm wide, superimposed load 20 kN/m, M25, Fe415) is redesigned by the limit state method. Compare the two designs and explain the difference.
outline: WSM result: section and steel
LSM: factored moment, depth from M<sub>u,lim</sub>
LSM steel and check
Comparison table of depth, concrete and steel
Reasons for the difference
What LSM must still check
answer: WSM design (from that question): 300 mm × 650 mm, d = 600 mm, 3 bars of 20 mm (942 mm²), service moment 111.9 kNm, stresses 8.00 and 218.8 N/mm².
LSM trial D = 500 mm (effective cover 50 mm, d = 450 mm). Self-weight 0.3 × 0.5 × 25 = 3.75 kN/m; total characteristic load 23.75 kN/m; M<sub>u</sub> = 1.5 × 23.75 × 6²/8 = 160.3 kNm.

Reason 1: WSM keeps concrete at 8.5 N/mm² (a third of f<sub>ck</sub>) under service load, so the depth is set by a low stress. LSM lets the concrete reach its design stress block at collapse, with the factor of safety put on the load (1.5) and on the materials (1.5 and 1.15) separately, so a smaller depth is enough.

Reason 2: a shallower beam has a smaller lever arm, so it needs more steel for the same moment; steel is used at 0.87f<sub>y</sub> = 361 N/mm² at collapse instead of 230 N/mm² at service, which limits that increase to 33 %.
Reason 3: the LSM beam is lighter, which reduces its own moment (160.3 against 1.5 × 111.9 = 167.9 kNm).

What LSM must still show: the slimmer beam has span/d = 6000/450 = 13.3, still below 20 so deflection should pass, and its service steel stress is higher, so crack width and bar spacing must be checked. These serviceability checks are what make the economy of LSM safe.
Conclusion: LSM saves about 23 % of the concrete for about 33 % more steel, and checks both collapse and serviceability, which is why IS 456 makes it the main method.

bank.q: A 7 m simply supported floor beam passes the collapse checks, but within two years it has sagged visibly and the partitions under it have cracked. Its calculated short-term deflection under the sustained load is 12 mm, the load came on at 28 days, and the shrinkage deflection is estimated at 4 mm. Evaluate the design with the limit state philosophy and recommend the checks and remedies.
outline: Collapse and serviceability are separate limit states
Long-term deflection with creep coefficient 1.6 and shrinkage
Compare with span/250 and span/350 or 20 mm
Causes: slenderness, early loading, high steel stress, cracking
Checks the designer missed
Remedies
answer: Passing the collapse checks shows only that the beam will not fail at 1.5 times the loads. Sagging and cracked partitions are failures of the limit state of serviceability, which has to be checked separately at service loads with γ<sub>f</sub> = 1.0 and γ<sub>m</sub> = 1.0.

Long-term deflection: creep multiplies the deflection under sustained load by about (1 + θ). For loading at 28 days θ = 1.6 (IS 456), so 12 × (1 + 1.6) = 31.2 mm. Adding shrinkage 4 mm gives a final deflection of about 35.2 mm. (This simple factor is an estimate; IS 456 Annex C uses an effective modulus E<sub>c</sub>/(1 + θ) in the same way.)

answer.text: Compare with the limits for L = 7000 mm:

head: limit
value
estimate
result
rows: creep 19.2 mm + shrinkage 4 mm = 23.2 mm (partitions built soon after loading)

answer: The deflection after partitions counts the part that happens after they are built; if the partitions went up soon after the load, nearly all the creep (1.6 × 12 = 19.2 mm) and shrinkage happen after them, which is enough to crack brick walls.

Likely causes: a slim section (a high span/effective depth ratio, possibly above the basic 20 times its modification factor); loading at an early age (had the load come on at 7 days θ would be 2.2 and the creep worse; at one year 1.1); high-grade steel used at a high service stress; and cracking, which lowers the stiffness well below that of the gross section.

Checks the designer should have made: the span/effective depth ratio with the modification factor for steel stress and compression steel; or a full deflection calculation with the cracked moment of inertia, creep and shrinkage; the crack width (0.3 mm general) and bar spacing; and the timing of the partitions.

Remedies for this beam: prop it and build the partitions after more of the creep has occurred; add a steel or concrete jacket or external plates to stiffen it; or provide flexible joints at the top of the partitions. For new designs: deeper sections, compression steel (it reduces creep deflection), later striking of formwork and loading, and good curing to reduce shrinkage.

Evaluation: the design is unsafe for use though safe against collapse. Limit state design exists to catch exactly this case, which neither the working stress method (which does not compute deflection) nor the ultimate load method (which ignores service behaviour) would have flagged.

glossary.def: A section in which concrete and steel reach their limits (permissible stresses in WSM, design strains in LSM) at the same time.
The load with a 95 % probability of not being exceeded during the life of the structure.
The strength below which not more than 5 % of test results are expected to fall.
The slow increase of strain in concrete under a sustained stress.
Final creep strain divided by elastic strain; 1.6 for concrete loaded at 28 days.
Characteristic strength divided by the partial safety factor for the material (0.446f<sub>ck</sub>, 0.87f<sub>y</sub>).
Distance from the extreme compression fibre to the centroid of the tension steel, d.
High yield strength deformed bar (Fe415, Fe500, Fe550), ribbed for bond, with yield taken as the 0.2 % proof stress.
Distance between the compression force C and the tension force T in a section.
A condition beyond which a structure or member no longer satisfies a design requirement.
Failure of a member by flexure, compression, shear or torsion, checked with factored loads.
Loss of fitness for use by deflection, cracking or vibration, checked with service loads.
The factor by which a service load is multiplied to get the ultimate load.
In WSM, m = 280/(3σ<sub>cbc</sub>), the factor that converts a steel area to an equivalent concrete area.
The line in a section where the bending strain is zero.
A section with more steel than the balanced amount; concrete fails first, suddenly.
A factor applied to a characteristic load (γ<sub>f</sub>) or strength (γ<sub>m</sub>) to obtain its design value.
The largest stress allowed at service load in the working stress method.
The stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.002 after unloading; the yield strength of bars with no sharp yield point.
Contraction of concrete as it dries, with no load; about 0.0003 strain.
The distribution of compressive stress in concrete at collapse, summarised by 0.36f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> acting at 0.42x<sub>u</sub>.
The mean strength a mix is designed for, f<sub>ck</sub> + 1.65s, so that its 5 % value reaches the grade.
A section with less steel than the balanced amount; steel yields first and the failure gives warning.
Design for collapse under service loads times a load factor, with materials at their full strength.
Elastic design that keeps service-load stresses within permissible stresses.
